READING 8
THE RETURN AND RISK OF A
FINANCIAL PORTFOLIO
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
This reading introduces modern portfolio theory. This material is the
basis for the Portfolio Construction topic area, and we will repeat much
of it there.
While the calculations are necessary (and testable on the exam), they are
there to support concepts that are quite straightforward. We will state
the basics of those concepts here, and develop them throughout this
reading and in Portfolio Construction. Keeping these key points in mind
as you go along will make it easier to grasp what the calculations are
telling us.
Risk, in the context we use it here, refers to variability of an asset’s or
portfolio’s rate of return. We measure it as the standard deviation of
returns. Defined this way, risk includes both upside and downside.
If an investment has no risk, we expect it to earn the risk-free rate of
return.
A single asset’s risk has two components: unsystematic risk that is
specific to that asset, and systematic risk that comes from the market in
which it exists.
Risk and expected return are a tradeoff. The more risk an investment
has, the more return an investor must expect the investment to provide,
for the investor to be willing to accept that risk.
If two investments have the same expected return, a rational investor
will prefer the one that has less risk. If two investments have the same
risk, a rational investor will prefer the one with a greater expected
return.

If two risky assets have rates of return that are not perfectly correlated,
it is possible to combine them in a portfolio that will have less risk than
the weighted average of the securities’ risks. This is the diversification
effect.
The diversification effect diminishes as we add more assets to a
portfolio. After about 30 assets, a portfolio’s risk and expected return
approach those of the overall market. At that point, we say a portfolio
has diversified away the unsystematic risk of the assets in it.
Because it is possible to diversify away unsystematic risk, the market
does not reward investors for taking it. Therefore, an asset’s expected
return only reflects its degree of exposure to the market (systematic
risk).
The best risk-return tradeoff an investor can achieve is some
combination of a fully diversified portfolio and a risk-free asset. What
combination is optimal depends on how risk averse an investor is.
MODULE 8.1: PORTFOLIO EXPECTED RETURN
LOS 8.a: Calculate, interpret, and evaluate the expected return, variance,
standard deviation, covariance, and correlation of portfolio returns.
Effective portfolio management depends on various types of portfolio statistics,
including expected returns, standard deviations, and correlations. These statistics
can either be historical (which factors in past risk and return information) or
forward-looking (which normally requires model-based forecasts).
Analysts can use historical returns to guide realistic expectations, but the data
may be biased if the history is not long. Forward-looking returns depend on
economic or financial forecasts, but these may incorporate historical
information. With either methodology, analysts must re-assess their expectations
regularly to see whether they need to make tactical or strategic adjustments.
The historical return of a portfolio for a period is simply the weighted average
of the realized returns for each asset in the portfolio:

If we are evaluating multiple periods, we must incorporate the cumulative return
of the assets over all periods. If we do not rebalance the portfolio during the
entire time period (T), the cumulative portfolio return remains simply the
weighted average of the assets’ returns over the period, using the initial
weighting of each asset:
This cumulative return differs from the arithmetic average of returns across all of
these periods because the arithmetic average return does not incorporate
compounding.
To make the effect of compounding explicit, we can express a portfolio’s
compound return over T periods as follows:
This cumulative approach assumes no reallocation of capital, and that all
distributions are reinvested into the same asset.
The geometric average of the portfolio returns can be calculated as follows:
As the markets fluctuate over time, the weights of the individual assets in the
portfolio will change as some assets decline in value, while others increase or
stay the same. This is known as portfolio drift. Without rebalancing, over time
this can lead to style drift, where the portfolio moves out of alignment with its
original strategy. For example, in a portfolio that is meant to be balanced

between stocks and bonds, a strong equity market can result in an overweight
stock position.
Style drift can also occur if the individual holdings have changes to their
investment characteristics. One example is when a stock moves into a different
capitalization category due to the company’s growth, such as a small-cap stock
moving to the mid-cap category.
While portfolio drift might sometimes offset style drift, it is appropriate for a
portfolio manager to regularly monitor and rebalance holdings to ensure that a
portfolio is maintaining its original investment goals.
Because portfolio drift changes the weights for the various assets, return
calculations must be adjusted each period to reflect the new weightings. This is
the cumulative return for a portfolio with changing weights:
The arithmetic average with changing weights is calculated as follows:
This is the geometric or cumulative return over T periods:

EXAMPLE: Calculating returns with changing weights
Maya Rivera has been managing a two-asset portfolio for the past three
quarters. Rivera needs to show her client both their quarterly returns and the
cumulative return over this time frame. The initial allocation was $100 for each
asset. The individual returns for the assets are as follows:
Calculate the arithmetic and geometric returns over the three quarters.

Answer:
As mentioned, without rebalancing, a portfolio composition may deviate from its
original risk-return profile; this, in turn, will affect the portfolio’s performance.
The degree of impact will depend on the weighting approaches that were used in
the original allocation. With an equal-weighted portfolio, portfolio drift causes
securities with high returns to increase in weight and causes the portfolio’s
performance to become biased toward higher-growth or higher-volatility assets.
With a portfolio that is not equally weighted, portfolio drift causes assets with
large allocations to increase in weight. This causes the portfolio’s performance to

resemble that of a momentum-driven strategy, and it may also increase the
portfolio’s concentration risk.

MODULE 8.3: CORRELATION AND
DIVERSIFICATION BENEFITS
Changing the weightings of assets in a portfolio affects both its risk profile and
its expected returns. If the assets do not have a high correlation to each other,
combining the assets creates a diversification benefit that can help to reduce the
overall risk of the portfolio. This benefit is reflected in the concave shape of the
curve shown in Figure 8.1, which is a mix of various weights of the two assets in
the portfolio we used in our earlier example. Moving along the curve, note that
portfolio risk decreases more than the decrease in portfolio return.
Figure 8.1: Diversification Benefit Using Different Portfolio Weights
The curve shown in Figure 8.1 shows the risk and return characteristics of the
feasible portfolios an investor can create using these two assets. Of these
portfolios, the efficient set includes those that have the highest return for any
given level of risk.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
Later in this reading, we will use this concept to define the efficient
frontier from among portfolios that theoretically include all investable
assets.

Correlations between assets’ returns drive the risk-return relationship in
portfolios. Portfolio risk decreases as the correlation between the assets’ returns
decreases. That is, the lower the correlation of asset returns, the greater the risk
reduction (diversification) benefit of combining assets in a portfolio. If asset
returns were perfectly negatively correlated, portfolio risk could be eliminated
altogether for a specific set of asset weights.
We show these relations graphically in Figure 8.2 by plotting the portfolio risk
and return for all portfolios of two risky assets, for specific values of the assets’
returns correlation.
Figure 8.2: Risk and Return for Different Values of ρ
Increasing the number of assets in the portfolio creates more complexity in
assessing its risk and return. For example, if we add a third asset, we need to
account for all the elements in the variance-covariance matrix shown in the
first panel of Figure 8.3. Adding a fourth asset increases the number of
covariances, as shown in the second panel.
Figure 8.3: Variance-Covariance Matrix for Three-Asset and Four-Asset Portfolios

The number of covariances increases exponentially as the portfolio size
increases. For a portfolio of N assets, the number of covariances is (N2 − N) / 2.
A portfolio of 30 assets has (900 − 30) / 2 = 435 unique covariances.
We can normalize a covariance matrix to create a correlation matrix. This
matrix can help investors identify which assets have the lowest returns
correlations and, thus, contribute to reducing overall portfolio risk.

Expected Portfolio Variance
We can express portfolio variance on a forward-looking basis, using assets’
expected returns and expected variances of returns. Portfolio returns can
incorporate different economic scenarios and their associated probabilities,
which sum to 1.

The first step is to calculate the portfolio’s expected return under each scenario,
which is the weighted average of the assets’ expected returns under that scenario.
Then, to arrive at the expected portfolio return across all scenarios, we take a
probability-weighted average of all the scenarios’ expected returns.
To calculate the expected portfolio variance, for each scenario we square the
deviation between the scenario’s expected return and the portfolio expected
return. We then multiply the result by the scenario’s probability. The sum of
these probability-weighted squared deviations gives us the expected variance.
where m represents a scenario in the model

= −3.50%
Next, weight the scenarios’ expected returns by their probabilities to get the
portfolio’s expected return:
E(rP) = 0.45 × 11.25% + 0.35 × 5.25% + 0.20 × −3.50% = 6.20%

Recession: (−3.50% − 6.2%)2 × 0.20 = 18.8180

As the number of assets in a portfolio increases, each asset’s contribution to the
total portfolio variance decreases. For an equally weighted portfolio with a large
number of assets, the variance of returns is approximately the product of the
average variance of its assets’ returns and their average correlation:

 The approximation should be

EXAMPLE: Estimating portfolio variance with a large number of assets
Sanford Asset Management is reviewing the annual statistics for their domestic
equity portfolio.
Number of assets = 75
Average correlation between the assets = 0.45
Average variance of individual assets = 0.15
Estimate the portfolio variance.
Answer:
The portfolio variance can be estimated as: 
0.45 × 0.15 = 0.0675 = 6.75%

Note: The more exact formula results in 6.86%.
A common rule in the investment management industry is that a portfolio of 20
to 30 well-chosen assets should capture most of the benefits of diversification. A
portfolio of uncorrelated assets reduces the risk that is specific to individual
assets, known as their unsystematic risk—but this does not eliminate the risk of
the broader market, or systematic risk. Beyond about 30 assets, the marginal
diversification benefit of each additional asset diminishes to near zero.

MODULE 8.4: THE MINIMUM-VARIANCE
PORTFOLIO AND THE EFFICIENT FRONTIER
LOS 8.b: Describe, calculate, and interpret the minimum-variance portfolio
and portfolios that lie on the efficient frontier.

Investors have constraints that limit which investments are appropriate to meet
their objectives. Chief among these constraints are their return requirements and
their preferred level of risk. Portfolio optimization works to find the most
advantageous combination of assets in a portfolio, given an investor’s return and
risk constraints.
This can involve many possible asset mixes that offer a wide range of risk and
return characteristics. Each of these individual feasible portfolios is considered a
risky portfolio, as each one has uncertain return and exposes the investor to
potential gains or losses.
For any given level of risk, one portfolio must offer a higher expected return
than any others. These optimal portfolios form the efficient frontier, which is
the upper bound of the feasible portfolios. Portfolios on the efficient frontier
represent the highest expected return for a given level of risk.
By contrast, portfolios that have the lowest risk for a given level of expected
return form the minimum-variance frontier. The efficient frontier is the
segment of the minimum-variance frontier that only includes efficient portfolios.
In Figure 8.4, the curved line to the left of the attainable portfolios is the
minimum-variance frontier, and the solid segment of the curve is the efficient
frontier.
The area to the left of the minimum-variance frontier (and above the efficient
frontier) represents risk-return combinations that cannot be created with the
available set of assets.
Figure 8.4: Feasible Portfolios and Efficient Frontier

In a simple case of a portfolio with only two risky assets, we can calculate the
weights of each asset that will form the minimum-variance portfolio. If we know
the returns variance of each asset

Answer:

the S&P 500 (Asset A):
In a theoretical portfolio that includes all investable assets, the minimum-
variance portfolio is known as the global minimum-variance portfolio, and the
portfolios that have the highest expected return for each level of risk make up the

Adding a Risk-Free Asset
So far, we have been discussing portfolios that only consist of risky assets. Next,
we consider how an investor can select an optimal portfolio if a risk-free asset,
one that has zero variance of returns and earns the risk-free rate of return, can be
combined with a portfolio of risky assets.
As we show in Figure 8.5, the risk-free asset lies on the vertical axis (zero risk).
If we draw a straight line from the risk-free asset that intersects the efficient
frontier at exactly one point (i.e., is tangent to the efficient frontier), that point
denotes the optimal risky portfolio (also known as the tangency portfolio).
Figure 8.5: Optimal Risky Portfolio With a Risk-Free Asset

The tangency portfolio is “optimal” in the sense that it is the efficient portfolio
with the greatest Sharpe ratio, or excess expected return (above the risk-free
rate) per unit of risk:
By combining a risky portfolio with the risk-free asset, investors can create a
range of portfolios, shown by the straight line in Figure 8.5 (which we will
define later in this reading as the capital allocation line associated with this risky
asset), and select the one that best reflects their desired risk-return profile. The
expected return on the combined portfolio is a weighted average of the risky
portfolio’s expected return and the risk-free rate of return.
Portfolios to the left of the tangency portfolio have weights between zero and
100% for the risk-free asset and the risky asset, and represent combinations of
risk-free lending and investing in the tangency portfolio.
Portfolios to the right of the tangency portfolio have negative weights of the
risk-free asset and weights greater than 100% in the risky asset, which
represent borrowing at the risk-free rate and investing the borrowed funds in
the tangency portfolio.
Because the risk-free asset has zero standard deviation of returns—and,
therefore, zero correlation with a risky portfolio’s returns—the standard
deviation of the combined portfolio is simply the weight of the risky portfolio
times its standard deviation of returns.

Portfolio Optimization
Approaches to selecting the most efficient allocation of assets for a portfolio
include the following:
Return-constrained optimization. This minimizes portfolio risk for a given
level of return.
Risk-constrained optimization. This finds the highest expected return for a
given level of risk and will identify combinations of portfolios that lie on the
efficient frontier.
Risk-adjusted return optimization. This maximizes the Sharpe ratio.

The key inputs into the portfolio optimization process are as follows:
Expected returns for each individual asset, which can be forecast based on their
short-term or long-term historical performance, incorporating economic and
financial indicators, industry trends, and company-specific factors
Volatility for each asset, which is commonly measured as the standard
deviation of returns and can be determined based on historical data or forward-
looking expectations
Asset correlations, which quantify the co-movements between asset returns
Investor-specific factors also come into play with portfolio optimization. An
investor’s risk tolerance, which is their ability and willingness to absorb losses,
plays a key role in asset selection, as does an investor’s time horizon and cash
return requirements. Other examples of portfolio constraints include asset types,
limits on exposure to individual assets and sectors, and nonnegative asset
weights (i.e., no short selling, or borrowing a security to sell and then
repurchase later). Such constraints may move the asset weights away from their
otherwise optimal combination.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
We will discuss investors’ requirements and constraints in more detail in
the Portfolio Construction topic area.

MODULE 8.5: RISK AVERSION
LOS 8.c: Explain the selection of an optimal portfolio, given an investor’s
risk aversion and the capital allocation line, and how this extends to the
market portfolio and the capital market line.
The theory behind selecting an optimal investment portfolio rests on several key
assumptions:
Investors are rational and risk averse. All investors make decisions aimed at
maximizing their satisfaction (utility). They prefer higher returns and lower
risk. They will choose investments that offer the best risk-return tradeoff
according to their preferences.
Investors have a single-period time horizon. They will make an investment
decision at the beginning of a period and evaluate their results at the end of that
period.
There are no taxes or transaction costs. This simplifies the analysis to focus
solely on investment performance and market behavior.
A risk-free asset can be purchased or sold. Investors can borrow and lend at a
constant risk-free rate.
Investor Risk Preferences
An individual’s attitude toward risk when making investment decisions is known
as his risk preference. This preference determines how much risk (variability in
returns) an individual is willing to assume in exchange for potentially larger
gains. We can divide possible risk preferences into three categories:
Risk seeking. These are investors who prefer uncertain outcomes over
guaranteed outcomes. They derive extra utility from the uncertainty of their
investment and may even be willing to accept a lower return. A common
example of risk-seeking is gambling in casinos, where the expected return is
usually negative.
Risk neutral. These are investors who are indifferent between an uncertain
outcome and a guaranteed outcome with the same expected value. A risk-
neutral investor would focus on returns only, without regard to the level of risk.
This is a more common attitude when an investment represents a small fraction
of an individual’s overall wealth.

Risk averse. These investors prefer guaranteed outcomes over uncertainty, even
if a gamble has a high expected value. They aim to minimize risk for a given
level of return.
Most real-world investors fall into the risk-averse category. However, risk-
neutral investors can offer insights in theoretical settings. This kind of research
focuses on large institutional investors that execute large numbers of small
transactions. Over time, the variance of their trades averages out and renders
their expected return nearly certain.
Utility Functions
We can characterize an investor’s preferences as a utility function that factors in
both expected return and risk. While several forms of investor utility functions
have been posited, a typical utility function might be expressed as follows:
The more risk averse an investor is, the greater the A in the investor’s utility
function. While a risk-neutral investor would have an A equal to zero and a risk-
seeking investor would have a negative A, portfolio theory assumes all investors
are risk averse (A greater than zero). Research suggests investors’ coefficients of
risk aversion tend to be between 2 and 3 and are rarely below 1.
Another way of expressing a utility function is mean-variance utility, which
represents an investor’s preferences regarding only two factors, expected return
and risk:
This function ignores other factors, such as an investor’s total wealth, that are
thought to affect an investor’s behavior in economic theory.
Risk preference relates closely to the concept of risk tolerance, which is the
extent to which an investor is willing to accept risk to achieve greater expected
return. Risk tolerance is the inverse of risk aversion: the lower the risk aversion,
the higher the risk tolerance.

An individual’s risk tolerance tends to change over time due to factors such as
age, wealth level, and the state of the economy. Risk tolerance also varies across
countries and cultures.
Approaches to observing investors’ risk aversion include absolute risk
aversion, which refers to how an investor’s utility changes with each increment
of additional risk, assuming the investor’s wealth remains constant; or relative
risk aversion, which assumes an investor’s wealth changes and observes how
this affects the proportion of their wealth an investor is willing to risk.
Indifference Curves
An indifference curve is a tool from economics that, in this application, plots
combinations of risk (standard deviation) and expected returns among which an
investor is indifferent. In constructing indifference curves for portfolios based on
only their expected return and standard deviation of returns, we are assuming
that these are the only portfolio characteristics that investors care about.
In Figure 8.6, we show three indifference curves for a risk-averse investor. The
investor’s expected utility is the same for all points (portfolios) along any single
indifference curve. Portfolios along indifference curve I1 in Figure 8.6 are
preferred to all portfolios along I2, which are preferred to all portfolios along I3.
Figure 8.6: Risk-Averse Investor’s Indifference Curves

The slope of the indifference curves represents an investor’s degree of risk
aversion, or how much additional risk an investor is willing to take on for
additional return while maintaining the same level of utility. A steeper slope
implies greater risk aversion. A theoretically risk-neutral investor would have
flat indifference curves, while a risk-seeking investor’s indifference curves
would slope downward.

MODULE 8.6: CAPITAL ALLOCATION LINE AND
CAPITAL MARKET LINE
As we saw earlier in this reading, we can combine a risk-free asset with a risky
portfolio to expand an investor’s opportunity set beyond the efficient frontier of
risky assets. This combined portfolio has an expected return that is the weighted
average of the expected returns on the risky portfolio and the risk-free asset, and
a standard deviation that is the weight of the risky portfolio times its standard
deviation of returns.
When we do this, we assume the following:

The risk-free asset has zero standard deviation of returns.
The standard deviation and expected return of the risky portfolio are both
greater than the risk-free rate.
The risk-free asset and the risky tangency portfolio are the only two assets
available to the investor.

Capital Market Line
The capital market line (CML) is a special case of a CAL, in which the risky
asset (tangency portfolio) is the market portfolio. The market portfolio consists
of all risky assets weighted by their market values. The market portfolio is said
to be mean-variance efficient, in that it has the highest Sharpe ratio of any
possible portfolio. The mutual fund theorem posits that combining a risk-free
asset with the market portfolio results in an efficient portfolio for all investors.
A major difference between a CAL and the CML is that a CAL assumes
investors have heterogenous expectations of assets’ expected returns, variances,
and covariances, while the CML assumes investors have homogeneous
expectations. The implication is that each investor would have a unique CAL,
depending on their expectations, but the CML is the same for all investors.
Clearly, a market portfolio that “contains all investable assets” is impossible to
achieve. In practice, investors rely on broad stock market indexes to represent
the market portfolio.

MODULE 8.7: THE CAPITAL ASSET PRICING
MODEL
When an investor diversifies across assets that are not perfectly correlated, the
portfolio’s risk is less than the weighted average of the risks of the individual

securities in the portfolio. The risk that is eliminated by diversification is called
unsystematic risk (also called unique, diversifiable, or firm-specific risk).
Because the market portfolio contains all risky assets, it must be a well-
diversified portfolio. All the risk that can be diversified away has been. The risk
that remains cannot be diversified away and is called systematic risk (also
called nondiversifiable risk or market risk).
You don’t actually have to buy all the securities in the market to diversify away
unsystematic risk. As you increase the number of stocks in a portfolio, the
portfolio’s risk falls toward the level of market risk. After 30 or so securities, the
portfolio standard deviation remains approximately constant. The remaining risk
is systematic, or nondiversifiable, risk. Figure 8.11 provides a general
representation of this concept.
Figure 8.11: Risk vs. Number of Portfolio Assets
Investment managers use return-generating models to estimate the expected
returns of risky securities based on specific factors. Some models (which we will
examine later in the Level I curriculum) use macroeconomic factors such as
GDP growth, inflation, or consumer confidence, along with fundamental factors
such as earnings, earnings growth, firm size, and research expenditures.
A widely used return generating model is the capital asset pricing model
(CAPM). This model estimates expected return based on a single factor, which
is an asset’s degree of exposure to systematic or nondiversifiable risk.

The CAPM makes the following assumptions:
All investors have homogeneous expectations for assets’ expected returns,
standard deviation of returns, and returns correlations between assets.
Investors choose the portfolio on the efficient frontier, based on their individual
preferences, with the risk and return combination that maximizes their
expected utility.
Investors take the market price as given, and no investor can influence prices
with their trades.
Markets are in equilibrium (i.e., there are no mispriced assets).

Portfolio Theory Limitations
While the models we have introduced here provide insight into portfolio
optimization, several of their underlying assumptions may not hold true in
reality:
Evidence does not support the idea that financial asset returns follow a normal
distribution; instead, they tend to show significant skewness and kurtosis.
Correlations among assets’ returns do not remain stable over time—especially
not at times of market stress.
Financial markets are less than perfectly efficient. Information asymmetries
can result in mispriced assets.
The models are highly sensitive to estimation errors. This can result in
incorrect weighting of assets in a portfolio.

Future returns and variances may not reflect their past behavior because of
changing market expectations or changes to the assets themselves.
Portfolio management also has practical constraints that are not incorporated into
modern portfolio theory:
Portfolio rebalancing strategies can be unrealistic if they do not account for
transactions costs.
Taxes can vary across portfolios due to both capital distributions and capital
appreciation. Taxes can change the optimal composition of a portfolio
significantly.
After-tax and risk-adjusted realized returns will be affected if a portfolio
manager takes advantage of capital losses to reduce capital gains.
